questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of a marketing objective?
options: A specific, measurable marketing target the business sets
The long-term plan for achieving marketing targets
The combination of product, price, promotion and place
The total amount spent on advertising in a year
questions.why: An objective is the target itself, and a good one is measurable with a deadline, such as raising market share by 5% in a year.
whyNot: That is the marketing strategy. The strategy is how you reach the objective.
That is the marketing mix, which is the set of tools used day to day.
That is the promotion budget, an input rather than a target.

questions.stem: Which term is defined as: the long-term plan a business uses to achieve its marketing objectives?
options: Marketing strategy
Marketing mix
Marketing objective
Market research
questions.why: Strategy sits between the objective and the mix: it is the chosen route, such as moving into a premium segment and selling online.
whyNot: The mix is the four tools (product, price, promotion, place) used to carry out the strategy.
The objective is the target the strategy aims at, not the plan itself.
Research gathers information to inform the strategy; it is not the plan.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of an extension strategy?
options: An action taken to lengthen a product's life and delay its decline
A plan to enter a completely new industry
Increasing the price of a product in maturity
Withdrawing a product from the market
questions.why: Extension keeps an existing product selling for longer, through new variants, new packaging, a new market or a new use.
whyNot: That is diversification, which is about new products in new markets rather than extending an existing one.
A price change is one possible tactic, but extension is the broader aim of delaying decline.
Withdrawal is what extension is designed to postpone.

questions.stem: In the Boston Matrix, a product with a high market share in a high growth market is a:
options: star
cash cow
question mark
dog
questions.why: High share and high growth makes it a star. It needs continued investment to hold position, and should become a cash cow as the market matures.
whyNot: A cash cow has a high share in a LOW growth market, so it generates surplus cash.
A question mark has a LOW share in a high growth market.
A dog has a low share in a low growth market.

questions.stem: In the Boston Matrix, a cash cow is a product with:
options: a high market share in a low growth market
a high market share in a high growth market
a low market share in a high growth market
a low market share in a low growth market
questions.why: A cash cow dominates a mature market. It needs little investment because the market is not growing, so it throws off cash that can fund stars and question marks.
whyNot: That is a star, which needs heavy investment to defend its position in a fast-growing market.
That is a question mark, whose future is uncertain.
That is a dog.

questions.stem: Which statement about the product life cycle is correct?
options: Cash flow and sales do not follow the same shape
Cash flow and sales are always identical
Cash flow is at its highest during the introduction stage
Sales are highest during development
questions.why: A product in growth can be selling strongly while still consuming cash, because it needs stock, staff and promotion. The divergence between the sales curve and the cash flow curve is a standard exam point.
whyNot: They differ. Drawing them as the same curve is a common error.
Introduction has heavy promotion costs and low sales, so cash flow is usually negative.
Development has no sales at all, only costs.

questions.stem: Which stage of the product life cycle is usually the most profitable?
options: Maturity
Introduction
Development
Decline
questions.why: In maturity, sales are high and flat while development and launch costs have already been paid, so cash flow is strongly positive. This is why businesses work hard to extend it.
whyNot: Introduction combines low sales with heavy promotional spending, so it is normally loss-making.
Development generates no revenue at all.
Decline means falling sales and falling margins.

questions.stem: A business has a low market share in a fast growing market. What does the Boston Matrix suggest it faces?
options: A decision: invest to build share, or withdraw
A guaranteed route to becoming a cash cow
An immediate withdrawal, as it is a dog
No action, since the market is growing anyway
questions.why: That is a question mark. It could become a star with enough investment, or slide into a dog without it, so the matrix flags it as a genuine decision point rather than an answer.
whyNot: Nothing is guaranteed. A question mark only becomes a cash cow if it first wins share and the market then matures.
A dog has a low share in a LOW growth market. This market is growing.
Market growth attracts competitors, so standing still usually means losing share.

questions.stem: Why might a business keep a product classified as a dog?
options: It may complete a range that key customers or retailers expect
Dogs always generate the most cash
The Boston Matrix requires every quadrant to be filled
Dogs are always the most profitable products
questions.why: The matrix uses only two measures. A low-share product in a flat market may still be profitable, or may be needed so that a retailer stocks the rest of your range. Saying this is how you get evaluation marks.
whyNot: Cash cows generate the most surplus cash, not dogs.
The matrix is a description, not a rule. Nothing requires a business to hold a product in each quadrant.
Dogs are usually the least attractive. Some are profitable, but not as a rule.

questions.stem: Which marketing approach is most appropriate for a business to business (B2B) market?
options: Personal selling, technical specification and negotiated prices
Mass television advertising and emotional branding
Social media influencer campaigns aimed at teenagers
Psychological pricing such as $9.99
questions.why: B2B markets have fewer, larger customers who buy rationally, often by committee, on reliability, service and total cost. Relationships and specification matter far more than mass advertising.
whyNot: Mass advertising and emotional appeals suit B2C markets with many small consumers.
Influencer campaigns target individual consumers, not procurement departments.
Psychological pricing works on individual consumers, not on a business buyer comparing quotes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of a product portfolio?
options: The full range of products a business sells
The documents a business keeps about its customers
The share of the market a business holds
The stages a product passes through over time
questions.why: The portfolio is everything the business sells. The Boston Matrix is a way of analysing the balance of that portfolio.
whyNot: That is customer records or a database, not a portfolio in this sense.
That is market share.
That is the product life cycle.

questions.stem: A business finds all of its products are cash cows. What is the main risk?
options: It has nothing positioned in growing markets, so it has no future growth
It will run out of cash immediately
Its products will all move into the introduction stage
It cannot calculate market share
questions.why: Cash cows sit in low growth markets. A portfolio made entirely of them produces cash now but has nothing being built for when those markets decline. A balanced portfolio uses cash cow money to fund stars and question marks.
whyNot: The opposite: cash cows generate surplus cash. The problem is the future, not current liquidity.
Products move forward through the life cycle, not back to introduction.
Share can still be calculated. The issue is strategic balance.

questions.stem: What is the most significant limitation of the Boston Matrix?
options: It uses only two measures and ignores profitability, brand and how products support each other
It can only be used by businesses with exactly four products
It requires the market to be growing
It cannot be drawn without a computer
questions.why: Relative share and market growth are useful but narrow. A product can look like a dog and be highly profitable, or look like a star and be losing money. The matrix is a starting point for a conversation, not a decision.
whyNot: It works with any number of products.
It handles low growth markets explicitly: that is what the bottom half of the matrix is.
It is a two-by-two grid drawn in seconds on paper.

questions.stem: An extension strategy is most likely to fail when:
options: consumer tastes have genuinely moved away from the product
the product is in the maturity stage
the business has cash available to invest
the product has a strong brand
questions.why: Extension delays decline caused by market saturation. It cannot rescue a product whose underlying demand has gone, as DVD rental found. Then extension is money spent postponing the inevitable.
whyNot: Maturity is exactly when extension strategies are used, and when they work best.
Available cash makes extension easier, not harder.
A strong brand makes extension more likely to succeed, because customers will try the new variant.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders objective, strategy and mix for a business aiming to grow share?
options: Objective: raise share to 9%. Strategy: move into the premium segment online. Mix: redesign the product, raise the price, advertise on social media, sell direct.
Objective: advertise on social media. Strategy: raise share to 9%. Mix: move into the premium segment.
Objective: redesign the product. Strategy: raise the price. Mix: raise share to 9%.
Objective, strategy and mix all mean the same thing in marketing.
questions.why: The target comes first, the route second, the tools third. Getting this hierarchy right is often worth a mark in itself and stops answers drifting.
whyNot: This puts a tool (advertising) as the objective and the target as the strategy.
This puts tools as the objective and strategy, and the target as the mix.
They are three distinct levels, and examiners test whether you can tell them apart.

questions.stem: How does building customer loyalty affect price elasticity of demand?
options: It makes demand less price elastic, because loyal customers are less willing to switch
It makes demand more price elastic
It has no effect on elasticity
It makes demand perfectly elastic
questions.why: Loyalty means fewer customers leave when the price rises, so demand becomes less responsive to price. That is precisely why businesses invest in loyalty schemes and brand building.
whyNot: More elastic would mean customers leave more readily, which is the opposite of loyalty.
Elasticity depends on willingness to switch, and loyalty is exactly what reduces that willingness.
Perfectly elastic demand means any price rise loses every customer, which no loyal base looks like.
